title: MGA submission automation software: buy for accuracy, not speed
summary: How to evaluate MGA submission automation software: eight criteria, four of them MGA-specific, and why field-level accuracy decides your capacity renewals.
body_markdown:
MGA submission automation software is best judged on accuracy, because in 2026 your capacity providers renew you on loss ratio and pay far less attention to turnaround time. MGA premium is growing fast. According to AM Best, US MGAs wrote $108.7B in direct premiums in 2025, up 17.8% from the year before, which was the fifth straight year of double-digit growth, while the wider US property and casualty market grew about 5% over the same year. MGAs are taking share, although the terms behind that growth are tightening, since carriers and reinsurers want loss-ratio stability and cleaner data before they extend capacity. That shift changes what the software is for, because submission automation now works as a capacity control, and the factor that decides the purchase is field-level accuracy. A misread number never stays in the document, and it follows the risk into your pricing, your loss pick and the reports your capacity providers read.


According to AM Best, US MGA direct premium grew 17.8% to $108.7B in 2025, against about 5% growth for the wider US property and casualty market.


## Why is MGA submission automation a capacity decision first?


MGA submission automation is a capacity decision first because your capacity providers now underwrite your data as closely as your book, and record MGA growth has made them selective. As per Conning, total US MGA premium was near $128B for 2025, with fronting carriers behind about 20% of it, and those fronting and reinsurance providers are asking for shorter contracts and more data before they renew. The[delegated underwriting authority](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/delegated-underwriting-authority) you hold depends on that data holding up.


Rates will not cover a mistake for you, since commercial pricing is soft in 2026 and, according to WTW, aggregate commercial rates moved about 0.5% in the second quarter of 2026. In a soft market you cannot re-rate your way out of a risk you mispriced at intake, so a wrong exposure or loss figure prices the account low, your capacity provider sees the result in the later reporting, and the next step is often a cut to your authority or your commission.


## What breaks when the software optimizes for speed alone?


When software optimizes for speed alone, it moves the wrong number first, and accuracy is what protects the loss ratio. Fast extraction without validation drops or misreads fields, and accuracy then decays across formats, because submissions arrive in hundreds of broker and carrier layouts, so the tool clears the easy ones and guesses on the rest without telling anyone.


The cost lands on the P&L. A single misread loss total or vehicle count misprices the account, and on a book priced off that data, a 5% field error rate becomes a loss-ratio problem you discover a year later. We explain the math in[why 95% extraction accuracy is not production ready](https://pibit.ai/blog/underwriting-accuracy-commercial-pc-95-percent-production-ready) . The mechanism that holds accuracy is review around the model, and Pibit AI pairs AI extraction with expert validation and guarantees 99.9% field-level accuracy with our human-in-the-loop, so low-confidence fields route to a person while the rest clear fast.


## Which criteria matter when you evaluate MGA submission automation software?


An MGA should weigh eight criteria when it evaluates submission automation software, and each one maps to a capacity or loss-ratio risk you already own.


Evaluation criterion What good looks like What should make you walk


Field-level accuracy A contractual field-level SLA with penalties A "best effort" or model-average accuracy number


Exception handling AI plus expert validation on low-confidence fields Auto-clear with no human check on low-confidence data


Multi-carrier appetite routing Coded appetite per capacity provider, routed automatically One generic appetite and manual re-routing


Delegated authority audit trail Every field linked back to its source document No provenance and no data lineage


Output Clean, normalized reporting back to each capacity provider Manual spreadsheet rekeying before reporting


Integration path Headless API that layers on Guidewire, Duck Creek, or Insurity A forced system migration


Pricing model Priced on submissions received, bought module by module Per-document guesswork or an all-or-nothing bundle


Time to implement A module live in a few weeks A multi-quarter build


Four of these criteria are specific to MGAs:


- You run more than one capacity provider, so appetite routing has to be coded per carrier.
- You hold delegated authority, so every field needs[field-level provenance](https://pibit.ai/blog/field-level-provenance-ai-underwriting-audit-standard) your providers can audit.
- You owe each carrier a report, so normalized output has to be built in.
- Your authority rests on clean data, so per-program model isolation keeps each provider's data and rules apart.


## How should an MGA weigh speed against accuracy?


An MGA should treat speed as a constraint and accuracy as the goal, because brokers still send the next account to whoever answers first, while speed on wrong data loses money twice: you carry the mispriced risk, and you put at risk the capacity that lets you write it. The human-in-the-loop model gives you both, since fields the AI is sure of move straight on and the few uncertain ones get a person before they reach a quote, with results back within two hours at most in Verified mode. We cover how fast clearance really needs to be in our piece on[submission intake automation](https://pibit.ai/blog/submission-intake-automation-insurance) .


It also helps to be honest about the edge cases. Some submissions should never clear unattended, such as complex schedules, conflicting loss runs and delegated-authority exceptions, and a tool that hides those behind an auto-clear rate is selling you speed you will pay for later.

The safest rollout starts with one program and one document type, so you can prove the loss-ratio case before you expand. Your stack stays in place, since a headless, API-first layer sits on top of your existing policy admin system with no rip-and-replace and no retraining, and a module goes live in a few weeks. Per-program model isolation keeps each capacity provider's data and rules separate, which matters when you answer to several carriers at once.
